Kill Switch

Chop your signal in rhythm, a different one in each ear.

A stereo rhythmic kill-switch effect with 20 patterns and endings for the end of a song, for MOD Dwarf, MOD Duo X and MOD Duo

20 patterns + your ownStereo rows5 endingsMomentary footswitch

Kill Switch

OverviewQuick startThe plugin on the pedalboardInteractive manualThe patternsThe endingsYour own patternPlaying it liveFactory presetsTipsQuestions & answers
Store pageSource code

Kill Switch chops your signal in a rhythm, like the momentary kill switch some guitars have: while the effect is on, a looping pattern lets the sound through or cuts it, in time with the tempo you set. It is stereo: the left and the right side each have a row of steps of their own, so the sound can change with the side: a ping-pong from ear to ear, one ear chopped while the other one stays, a swell that moves across. Played from a single guitar, with Mono on, it is the plain kill switch.

It has two families of effects:

  • Patterns loop for as long as the effect is on. Twenty to choose from (ten with the same row on both sides, ten for a stereo sound), and your own, written on the settings page, with three levels per step.
  • Endings are for the end of a song. They play once when you switch the effect on and finish in silence: a bouncing ball, a helicopter that lands, a stutter that dies away. You choose them; you do not draw them.

The effect is on while Kill is: a footswitch that is momentary by default, so it chops only while you hold it.

01

Quick start

You need a pedalboard with an audio input and an output, and a guitar (or any sound) going through it.

  1. Add Kill Switch to your pedalboard and put it between your guitar input and the rest of the chain (or between the amp and the output). It has two audio inputs and two audio outputs, one pair for each side.
  2. Feed both sides. A single instrument is mono: turn on Mono on the plugin, and the left input feeds both sides. With a stereo source (a stereo pedal before it, an amp with a stereo send), leave Mono off and connect each side to its own input.
  3. Turn it on. The plugin starts off: your sound passes clean, and the label over the footswitch says Kill. Tap the footswitch on the screen and the light over it turns red: play a note and it is chopped at once. Tap again to go back to clean. (From step 7 on, your device's footswitch does it.)

  4. Choose a pattern with the arrows on each side of its name. Under the name there is a row for the Left side (white) and one for the Right side (red): a bright square lets the signal through, a dark one cuts it. The first ten patterns have the same row on both sides.

  5. Set the tempo with − and + (hold one to go on) and pick the speed. Depth is how much of the signal a cut removes (100% is silence) and Edge is how long a cut takes to close and open.

  6. Try an ending. Tap Endings under the name, pick one with the arrows and set its length, then switch the effect off and on again: the ending plays once, from the start.

  7. Put it under your foot. Open the settings (Edit) and press the small button beside Kill in the top bar to assign it to a device footswitch. The dialog comes with Momentary already chosen: the effect is on only while you hold the footswitch (section 7).

Everything starts the moment you switch the effect on

A pattern starts again from its first step, and an ending starts from its beginning, every time Kill goes from off to on. Press the footswitch in time with the beat and the chops fall where you want them; press it as the last chord rings and the ending falls on it.

02

The plugin on the pedalboard

Item What it does
Patterns / Endings The family that plays. The tabs are in the column of the footswitch.
The arrows and the name Choose the pattern (section 4) or, in Endings, the ending (section 5). The arrows go round. In Patterns the last one is Custom, the one you write.
The two rows, L and R What each side does. In Patterns, a bright square lets the signal through, a dark one cuts it, a darker colour is the middle level; a pattern shorter than sixteen steps is repeated, the first run bright and the repetitions dimmer. In Endings, the whole ending along its time: the brighter the column, the more open the side. They go dim while Kill is off.
Tempo: − and + From 40 to 240 BPM. Hold a button to keep going. Endings use it too: their length is counted in beats.
Speed (Patterns) ½x, 1x, 2x or 4x: multiplies the speed of the pattern without changing the tempo.
Length (Endings) How long the ending lasts, in beats, from 2 to 32. At 120 BPM, 8 beats are 4 seconds.
Depth From 0% to 100%: how much of the signal a cut removes. 100% is silence; lower values only dip the level.
Edge From 0.1 ms to 20 ms, on a logarithmic scale: how long a cut takes to close and to open again.
Mono On: the left input feeds both sides. Off: each side has its own input.
Edit Opens the settings page: everything on the plugin with more room, the steps of your own pattern and the controls to assign (section 6).
The footswitch and its light Kill. The ring and the light above it are red while the effect is on, and the label at the top says On or Off. A tap on it on the screen toggles it; a device footswitch assigned to it is momentary by default.
Audio jacks In L and In R on the left, Out L and Out R on the right.
03

Interactive manual

Here the plugin is the real one: the same interface, the same script, running inside the manual. Press Open the interactive manual under the picture to open it full screen (Esc or Close brings you back). Nothing you do is saved or sent anywhere, and Reset puts it back the way it starts.

  • Explore: tap any part of the plugin to read what it is for, or pick it from the list under the picture. Show areas outlines everything that can be tapped. Use the buttons at the top to switch between the plugin on the pedalboard and its settings page.
  • Guided tours: step-by-step walkthroughs of the common tasks. A finger shows where to tap. Go forward and back with Next and Back: every step says what is happening and shows it in the plugin.
04

The patterns

Each pattern is a loop of steps, and each side has its own row. In every step a side is either let through or cut (or, in the middle level, half); the plugin goes from one step to the next in time with the tempo, and from the last step back to the first. The grids show every pattern as sixteen steps (the shorter ones repeat), the left row in white and the right row in red. A lit square is a step that lets the signal through (the middle level of Seesaw is shown as lit too).

The same row on both sides

The first ten patterns are the single-channel kill switch: both sides do the same, so they are what you want from one guitar with Mono on.

12345678910111213141516
Chop 8ths
Chop 16ths
Triplet chop
Machine gun
Syncopated 3-3-2
Gallop

Generic grooves

Six patterns that fit any style. Chop 8ths and Chop 16ths are the plain on-off chop at those note values, Triplet chop does it in triplets, Machine gun is the same at thirty-second notes, Syncopated 3-3-2 is the Latin-flavoured grouping of eight steps (three, three and two) and Gallop is a short-short-long figure of four.

Steps per beat: Chop 8ths 2 · Chop 16ths 4 · Triplet chop 3 · Machine gun 8 · Syncopated 3-3-2 2 · Gallop 4

12345678910111213141516
Morello solo chop
Morello toggle solo
Greenwood chunk
Buckethead burst

Inspired by guitarists famous for the kill switch

Four longer, busier patterns named after players known for the kill switch. The rhythms are our approximation, not a transcription of anyone's playing: use them as a starting point and change the tempo, the speed, the depth and the edge until it fits your song.

Steps per beat: Morello solo chop 4 · Morello toggle solo 4 · Greenwood chunk 2 · Buckethead burst 8

A row for each side

The next nine have a different row for each side. They need a stereo sound: connect both inputs, or turn Mono on to give both sides the same signal.

Ping-pong: the sound goes from ear to ear

The classic: while the left ear is cut, the right one plays, and the other way round. Ping-pong 8ths and Ping-pong 16ths use those note values, Triplet pong does it in threes (the third step is cut on both sides).

Steps per beat: Ping-pong 8ths 2 · Ping-pong 16ths 4 · Triplet pong 3

12345678910111213141516
Half deaf: left · L
Half deaf: left · R
Half deaf: right · L
Half deaf: right · R

Half deaf: one ear is chopped, the other is not

One side chops while the other stays as it is. Half deaf: left chops the left ear, Half deaf: right the right one: the plugin is named after them.

Steps per beat: Half deaf: left 2 · Half deaf: right 2

Sides that answer each other

Gallop sides gallops from one side to the other; Stagger is a syncopated answer between the two; Seesaw uses the middle level, so that one side fades out while the other one swells in, like a seesaw; Syncopated sides is the 3-3-2 grouping of eight steps, a step apart on the two sides.

Steps per beat: Gallop sides 4 · Stagger 4 · Seesaw 2 · Syncopated sides 2

The length of a step is 60 / (tempo × steps per beat × speed) seconds. At 120 BPM, Chop 8ths has a step of 250 ms, Ping-pong 8ths the same, and Machine gun a step of 62.5 ms.

The tempo is the plugin's own

Kill Switch does not follow the tempo of the pedalboard or of a MIDI clock: set the tempo here, or assign it to a knob or to an expression pedal.

05

The endings

An ending is a one-time effect for the end of a song. It plays once, from the moment you switch the effect on (Kill), lasts Length beats at the Tempo, and then everything is cut: the sound ends, and stays silent until you switch the effect off and on again. The five endings are chosen, not drawn: you pick one, and set its length, the tempo, the depth and the edge. (With Depth below 100% the end is not fully silent: the cut only goes down to that level.)

Ending What it does
Bouncing ball tam------tam-----tam---tam--tam-tam-ta-ta-t-t-t-ttttt: the first hit is at once and every gap is 78% of the one before, so the hits pile up towards the end and turn into a buzz, on both sides. The hits get shorter with their gaps.
Helicopter The blades go to the left, then to the right, one after the other, starting at the pace of sixteenth notes; the gap between them grows by 12% each time and the sound fades out, like a helicopter landing.
Stutter out Sixteenth notes that stay open less and less, from 92% of each to almost nothing, until they stop. The right side is half a note behind the left one.
Side fade Eighth notes, half open. The left side fades out first (by 60% of the ending) and the right one is the last to go.
Ping-pong out Eighth notes, one to each side in turn, starting on the left, and every one quieter than the one before.

Changing the ending or the family while the effect is on starts the new one from its beginning, so you can try them without switching off.

06

Your own pattern

The last pattern, Custom, is yours. Click Edit on the plugin (or open its settings with the gear icon). The settings page has everything the plugin has, with more room. At the top, on every page, there are Mono, Kill (the footswitch of the effect) and the arrows that go from page to page; under them, a small strip with what plays: its name and the two rows of steps, only to look at.

The pages are:

  • Pattern: Patterns or Endings, and under it every pattern (or ending) to pick with one tap. On a small screen they come one at a time, as ‹ name ›, with the arrows on each side of the name. Right under the choice, what each side does, as LEDs, with the length and the steps per beat of your own pattern: the steps are always together with the choice.
  • Tempo and feel: the tempo (with its buttons and a slider), Speed (or Length, in Endings), Depth and Edge.
  • Saved presets.

On a screen with room, the pages share the screen; on a small one each has its own. The strip under the top bar tells what plays on all of them.

The LEDs show a white row for the left side and a red row for the right side. A step is dark when it cuts, lit up to half its height when it is at the middle level, and fully lit when it passes the signal; the number of a step is brighter when a beat begins there. The LEDs show the pattern twice (at most sixteen steps): the second run, drawn as outlines, is the pattern coming round again. Beside the name Preview is the note value of a step (8ths, 16ths, triplets...): it is what tells Chop 8ths, Chop 16ths, Triplet chop and Machine gun apart, since they have the same steps at different speeds.

To write your own pattern:

  1. Pick any pattern and tap one of its steps. A built-in pattern cannot be changed, so the plugin asks: Make your own pattern? Tap Define custom pattern: it becomes Custom and starts as a copy of the pattern you were on, with its length and its steps per beat. (Not now leaves everything as it was.) Choosing Custom in the list plays what Custom holds (its starting steps the first time, then what you wrote last) without the question.

  2. Tap the steps of the L row (white) and of the R row (red). A tap goes to the next level, round and round:

    Level What the step does
    Cut Lowers the signal by Depth: silence at 100%.
    Half Halfway between a cut and the whole signal: at Depth 100% half the level, at 50% three quarters of it.
    Pass Lets the signal through as it is.

  3. Set the length with − and +, from 1 to 16 steps, the same for both sides. They appear under the LEDs while Custom plays. Only the first steps are played, and a tap on an outlined step changes the step it repeats; the steps after the length are kept, so you can shorten a pattern and bring its end back.

  4. Set the steps per beat, from 1 to 8: with 2 a step is an eighth note, 4 a sixteenth, 3 a triplet, 1 a quarter note.
  5. Listen to it. Your pattern plays as soon as you define it, and it plays while Custom is the pattern chosen.

Start from a built-in pattern

To change a pattern of the list a little, pick it, tap a step and define the Custom pattern: you get the whole pattern (both rows, length and steps per beat) ready to be changed.

Your pattern is made of controls of the plugin, so it is saved with the pedalboard, with your own saved presets and with snapshots. The factory presets do not touch it. Use the arrows of the top bar (or swipe sideways) to go to the Saved presets. Next to each control, a small button (the faders icon) assigns it to a device control.

07

Playing it live

Every control of the plugin can be assigned to a device control (a footswitch, a knob, an expression pedal), the way you assign any parameter: open the settings of the plugin (the gear icon, or Edit) and click the small button (the faders icon) next to the control to assign: Mono and Kill in the top bar, Pattern or Ending (the one that matches what plays) beside the name, Mode beside Patterns and Endings, and Tempo, Speed, Length, Depth and Edge beside their names. The button fills in once the control is assigned.

Control Good to assign it to
Kill A footswitch. It comes as Momentary: the effect is on only while you hold the footswitch (the kill switch of a guitar: you press, it chops; you let go, it is clean). Choose Toggle in the dialog to turn it on and off with each press. For an ending, a press is the end of the song.
Mode A footswitch: patterns for the song, endings for its last bar.
Pattern, Ending A knob, or a footswitch that goes through them.
Tempo A knob, or an expression pedal.
Speed A footswitch: hold it for double speed, let go for normal.
Length A knob.
Depth A knob or an expression pedal: from a gentle tremolo to a full cut.
Edge A knob: from a hard chop to a soft swell.

Kill is not the bypass of the pedal

MOD UI's own bypass of the plugin is still there and works as for any plugin. The footswitch of Kill Switch is a control of its own, Kill, because MOD UI offers a toggle (not a momentary switch) when you assign its bypass, and a kill switch is meant to be held.

On the screen of the device

With the aLabs Starless image (Starless 19 or later) the MOD Dwarf and the MOD Duo X can show widgets of a plugin on their screens, drawn by the plugin itself. The stock MOD firmware does not have this: the plugin works the same there and simply shows nothing. On the MOD Duo there is no screen to draw on.

A widget is for looking, not for touching: nothing on the screen reacts to a finger or to a button of the device. What changes it are the controls you assigned to the plugin, as always; the widget follows them.

Placing the widget

  1. Open the Display dialog (the Device menu of MOD UI) and choose Stereo pattern in the list of widgets of the pedalboard.
  2. Place it on an area of the screen: a column above a knob, two or three columns, a footer, both footers or the whole screen on the Dwarf; a knob, two knobs, the four knobs, the encoder band, a footer, both footers or the whole screen on each display of the Duo X. The dialog only offers the areas that are big enough for it.
  3. The dialog offers to assign Mode, Pattern and Tempo to controls of the device (you can change them or leave them out), so you can change them from the same page.
  4. Save. It can be placed on more than one area at once (a column and a footer, or one on each display of the Duo X).

It draws what fits in the area it gets: a footer shows the bare essentials, the whole screen shows everything.

Stereo pattern

Shows the two sides, left (L) and right (R), one above the other, so you see what each ear is getting (with a pattern that is the same on both sides, two equal rows). It needs an area at least 14 pixels high: a footer of the Dwarf (10) or of the Duo X (8) is too small for two rows, and the dialog does not offer it there.

MOD Dwarf MOD Duo X What you see
One column · 40 × 37 Two knobs, one above the other · 64 × 30 The name of the pattern (or of the ending), the two rows L and R with the mark under the step that plays, and at the bottom the tempo and the Speed (or the length in beats and the word ENDING). What does not fit is left out.
Two columns · 82 × 37 The four knobs · 128 × 30 The same, with more room.
Three columns · 124 × 37 Encoder band and knobs · 128 × 47 The same, with taller rows.
Whole screen · 128 × 64 Whole screen · 128 × 64 The same, as big as the screen allows.
No area of this kind One knob · 64 × 16 Only the two rows, L and R, with the mark.
No area of this kind Two knobs side by side · 128 × 16 Only the two rows, wider.

In the Patterns mode each row is the steps of that side (tall bar: the signal passes; half-height bar: middle level; line: a cut) and the mark moves with the tempo. In the Endings mode each row is the curve of the ending along its time, from the moment the plugin is switched on to its end, and a dotted line moves across it: you see how much is left.

  • A pattern: the rows are different on each side; that is the point of the plugin.
  • An ending: a bouncing ball, a helicopter, a stutter... each draws its own curve; the dotted line is where the ending is now.
  • The ending is over: the line reaches the end and the widget says END (on a tall area); after that everything is cut until you switch the plugin off and on.
  • Off: the rows go grey and the widget says OFF (where there is room for the word).

All of them have the speed at 1x. The first four are named after a song and use a pattern in the style of its guitar part, at about its tempo; they are a starting point, not a copy.

09

Tips

Set the tempo to the song, then leave it

The patterns are in time with the tempo you set, not with the band. Adjust the number until the chops sit with the drums: a difference of one or two BPM is enough to drift off the beat over a bar. For an ending, the tempo and the length together say how long it lasts: leave it a little longer than the last chord.

Switch it on on the beat

The pattern restarts from its first step every time Kill goes on, and the first ten patterns start with a cut. Press the footswitch on the beat (or just before it) and the first chop lands exactly there.

Use Mono for a single guitar

With one instrument, turn Mono on: both sides get the signal, and the patterns show their sides. With Mono off and only the left input connected, the right side is silent, and a ping-pong has only one ear to play.

Half deaf for a wide stereo

Half deaf keeps one ear steady and chops the other, which makes a stereo sound feel as if it moved around while it stays in place. Put it after a stereo reverb or chorus.

Soften it with Depth

At 100% a cut is silence. At 40 to 60% the signal only dips, which sounds like a sharp tremolo, and fits a sound that should stay present (an ambient pad, a drive that you do not want to disappear).

Edge changes the character

Short edges (below 1 ms) are percussive: the sound is stopped as if a switch were flicked. Long edges (10 ms and more) turn the chop into a soft swell. On an ending, a long edge smooths the buzz at the end of the Bouncing ball.

Put it where you want the cut

Before a delay, the cut chops what goes into the delay and the repeats go on ringing; after the delay, the repeats are chopped too. Try both places.

Build your own from a built-in pattern

Pick the built-in pattern that is closest, tap one of its steps and define the Custom pattern: you get a copy to change a step or two. Use the middle level for a ghost note: a step that is there, but soft.

10

Questions & answers

Nothing is cut, I hear my guitar as it is.

Check that the label at the top of the plugin says On and the light above the footswitch is red: the plugin starts off. If the footswitch is assigned to a device control in Momentary mode, the effect is on only while you hold it.

I hear the left side only.

Turn Mono on, or connect your source to both inputs: with only the left input connected, the right side has nothing to play.

The ending is over and I hear nothing.

That is the end: an ending finishes in silence. Switch the effect off and on again to hear it from the beginning. To get your sound back as it was, switch it off.

The chops are not on the beat of my song.

The tempo is the plugin's own (section 4): set it by ear, or assign it to a knob. And switch the effect on on the beat: the pattern starts again from the beginning each time.

Does it add latency? Is it stereo?

No latency: the signal is only multiplied by a number that goes up and down. It is stereo: two inputs and two outputs. For a single guitar, turn Mono on.

I hear a click at each cut.

Make Edge longer. At 0.1 ms the signal is stopped almost at once, which can click on a low note.

How many steps and how many levels can my own pattern have?

Up to 16 steps for each side, each with three levels (cut, half and pass), at 1 to 8 steps per beat.

I tapped a step and nothing changed.

On a built-in pattern a tap asks first (Make your own pattern?): confirm (Define custom pattern) to get a Custom pattern whose steps you can change.

I edited my pattern and it did not change what I hear.

Check that the family is Patterns and the pattern is Custom (the name on the plugin says so). The first change you make switches both, but if you then chose another one (or a controller did), choose Custom again in the list.

Is my pattern saved?

Yes, with the pedalboard, your saved presets and the snapshots. It is not in the factory presets, and it is not shared between pedalboards: each plugin on each pedalboard has its own.

Does it change the level of my sound when it is on?

Not while a step lets the signal through (it passes unchanged): the level only goes down in the cuts (and, a little, in the half steps). So there is nothing to compensate with a volume control.

Why are some patterns named after guitarists?

They are inspired by guitarists known for the kill switch, as a way to find the rhythm: the steps are our approximation of the style, not a transcription, and the plugin has no connection with the players or with their songs.
